label: Bonus Class 3
title: Word Builders: Roots, Prefixes and Suffixes
bigIdea: English builds many new words like Lego, by adding pieces to the front and back of a word (happy → unhappy → unhappiness); Arabic weaves vowels and extra letters around a root (usually three letters) (ك ت ب → كاتب، مكتب، مكتبة). Know the pieces and you can understand words you have never seen.
bigIdeaAr: تبني الإنجليزية كثيراً من كلماتها الجديدة مثل الليغو، بإضافة قطع إلى أول الكلمة وآخرها (happy ← unhappy ← unhappiness)، أما العربية فتنسج الحركات وحروفاً زائدة حول جذر ثلاثي في الغالب (ك ت ب ← كاتب، مكتب، مكتبة). اعرف القطع تفهم كلمات لم ترها من قبل.
builtOn: Lesson 9: Countable and uncountable nouns (review): save, spend, earn, borrow, lend
Lesson 10: Superlatives (the biggest, the best): talented, skilled, impressive, outstanding, popular, unique, judge, applause
Lesson 11: Would like / want: order, prefer, suggest, recommend, request, choice, waiter
Lesson 12: Should / shouldn't: improve, advice, opinion, suggestion, warning, mistake, patience, habit
Bonus Class 1: the -s ending; Bonus Class 2: countable nouns

objectives.en: I can split a word into its morphemes (un + help + ful) and say what each piece means.
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أقسّم الكلمة إلى وحداتها الصرفية (un + help + ful) وأذكر معنى كل قطعة.

objectives.en: I can use the prefixes un- and re- and the suffixes -er, -est, -ful, -less, -ness, -ion and -ment to build new words.
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أستخدم السوابق un- و re- واللواحق -er و -est و -ful و -less و -ness و -ion و -ment لبناء كلمات جديدة.

objectives.en: I can apply the spelling changes: big → biggest, happy → happier, nice → nicest.
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أطبّق تغييرات الإملاء: big ← biggest و happy ← happier و nice ← nicest.

objectives.en: I can compare English affixes with Arabic roots and patterns (كاتب، مكتب، مكتبة).
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أقارن اللواحق والسوابق الإنجليزية بالجذور والأوزان العربية (كاتب، مكتب، مكتبة).

keyTerms.meaning: The smallest piece of a word that has meaning: un-, help, -ful.
The main part of a word that carries the core meaning: help in helpful.
A piece added to the front: un- (not), re- (again).
A piece added to the end: -ful, -less, -ness, -er.
In Arabic, a template of vowels and extra letters poured around a root: فاعِل، مَفْعَل، مَفْعُول.
Building words by gluing pieces in a line (English) vs weaving a pattern through the root (Arabic).

facts.en: A morpheme is the smallest piece of meaning. 'Unhelpful' has three: un (not) + help + ful (full of). 'Cat' has one. 'Cats' has two (cat + plural -s).
facts.ar: المورفيم أصغر قطعة لها معنى. كلمة unhelpful فيها ثلاث: un (ليس) + help + ful (مليء بـ). و cat فيها واحدة، و cats فيها اثنتان (cat + -s الجمع).

facts.en: English is mostly concatenative: it glues pieces in a line, like Lego bricks. The base usually stays visible: teach → teacher, kind → kindness, happy → unhappiness.
facts.ar: الإنجليزية في الغالب «إلصاقية»: تلصق القطع في خط واحد كقطع الليغو، ويبقى الأصل ظاهراً عادة: teach ← teacher و kind ← kindness.

facts.en: Arabic is famous for non-concatenative morphology: a root of (usually) three consonants carries the core idea, and patterns weave vowels and extra letters through it. ك-ت-ب (writing): كَتَبَ wrote, كاتِب writer, مَكْتوب written, مَكْتَب desk/office, مَكْتَبة library/bookshop, كِتاب book.
facts.ar: تشتهر العربية بالصرف «غير الخطّي»: جذر من ثلاثة حروف غالباً يحمل الفكرة الأساسية، والأوزان تنسج الحركات وحروفاً زائدة خلاله. ك-ت-ب: كَتَبَ، كاتِب، مَكْتوب، مَكْتَب، مَكْتَبة، كِتاب.

facts.en: Arabic patterns carry meaning like English suffixes do: فاعِل = the doer (كاتب، لاعب) ≈ English -er (writer, player); مَفْعول = the thing done (مكتوب) ≈ -ed/-en (written); مَفْعَل / مَفْعَلة = a place (ملعب، مدرسة، مكتبة).
facts.ar: الأوزان العربية تحمل معنى كما تحمله اللواحق الإنجليزية: فاعِل للفاعل ≈ -er، ومَفْعول لما وقع عليه الفعل ≈ -ed/-en، ومَفْعَل ومَفْعَلة للمكان (ملعب، مدرسة، مكتبة).

facts.en: Neither language is 100% one type. Arabic also adds pieces (ال، ـون، ـة، سـ), and English also changes vowels inside words (sing → sang, man → men, foot → feet), a small echo of the Arabic way.
facts.ar: لا توجد لغة من نوع واحد تماماً: العربية تضيف قطعاً أيضاً (ال، ـون، ـة، سـ)، والإنجليزية تغيّر الحركات داخل بعض الكلمات (sing ← sang و man ← men)، وهذا صدى صغير للطريقة العربية.

facts.en: One suffix can have two jobs: -er makes comparatives (bigger) and also people who do things (teacher, player). Same spelling, different morphemes. And -s has three jobs: plural, he/she/it, and possessive 's.
facts.ar: قد تكون للاحقة الواحدة وظيفتان: -er للمقارنة (bigger) ولمن يقوم بالفعل (teacher). الكتابة واحدة والمورفيم مختلف. و -s لها ثلاث وظائف: الجمع، و he/she/it، والملكية 's.

arabicBridge.english: write → writer; play → player (-er = person who does it)
arabicBridge.point: Same idea, different machine: English adds -er at the end; Arabic pours the root into the pattern فاعِل.
arabicBridge.pointAr: الفكرة واحدة والآلة مختلفة: الإنجليزية تضيف -er في الآخر، والعربية تصبّ الجذر في وزن فاعِل.

arabicBridge.english: play → playground; study → study room (compound or new word)
arabicBridge.arabic: لَعِبَ ← مَلْعَب؛ دَرَسَ ← مَدْرَسة (وزن مَفْعَل/مَفْعَلة للمكان)
arabicBridge.point: Arabic has a ready-made 'place' pattern. English usually makes a compound or uses a different word (school is not built from study).
arabicBridge.pointAr: في العربية وزن جاهز للمكان، أما الإنجليزية فتصنع كلمة مركّبة أو تستخدم كلمة مختلفة (school ليست مشتقة من study).

arabicBridge.arabic: غير سعيد، غير صبور / قليل الصبر
arabicBridge.point: Arabic says 'not' with a separate word (غير); English glues un- or im- onto the adjective to make one word.
arabicBridge.pointAr: العربية تنفي بكلمة منفصلة (غير)، والإنجليزية تلصق un- أو im- بالصفة لتصبح كلمة واحدة.

arabicBridge.arabic: مفيد / عاجز؛ حريص / مهمل (أو: كثير العناية / عديم العناية)
arabicBridge.point: Arabic often uses a completely different word or a phrase (عديم، كثير). English uses the matching pair -ful / -less on the same base.
arabicBridge.pointAr: العربية تستخدم غالباً كلمة مختلفة تماماً أو تركيباً (عديم، كثير)، أما الإنجليزية فتستخدم الزوج -ful / -less مع الأصل نفسه.

arabicBridge.point: Arabic changes the pattern (وزن أفعل); English adds -er/-est and sometimes changes the spelling (double g).
arabicBridge.pointAr: العربية تغيّر الوزن (أفعل)، والإنجليزية تضيف -er/-est وتغيّر الإملاء أحياناً (مضاعفة g).

commonErrors.wrong: He is the most big player.
commonErrors.why: Short adjectives take -est. Learners over-use most, perhaps copying Arabic phrases with الأكثر (الأكثر شهرة).

commonErrors.wrong: the bigest / the happyest / the niceest
commonErrors.right: the biggest / the happiest / the nicest
commonErrors.why: Spelling rules: double the last consonant after one short vowel (big → biggest), y → i (happy → happiest), drop the silent e (nice → nicest).

commonErrors.wrong: She is very not patient. / She is not happy person.
commonErrors.right: She is impatient. / She is an unhappy person.
commonErrors.why: Arabic غير is a separate word; English often uses a prefix: un-, im-.
Mixing word classes: use is a verb/noun; we need the adjective form useful (-ful makes adjectives).

commonErrors.wrong: I want to improvement my English.
commonErrors.right: I want to improve my English. / My English needs improvement.
commonErrors.why: Using the noun (with -ment) where a verb is needed. Arabic often uses a verbal noun here (أريد تحسينَ لغتي), so learners pick the English noun.

commonErrors.wrong: He is a very care driver.
commonErrors.right: He is a very careful driver.
commonErrors.why: Adjective needed before a noun: care + -ful.
Good is irregular (good, better, best): these forms come from different old words, so there is no rule to follow.

teacher: Digital morpheme cards on a shared whiteboard (Microsoft Whiteboard in Teams) or on the slide: bases (help, care, use, kind, happy, teach, play, read, write, improve, suggest, popular, patient) and affixes (un-, re-, im-, -er, -est, -ful, -less, -ness, -ion, -ment, -ed)
Slide: the ك-ت-ب family tree and the ل-ع-ب and د-ر-س families
Race timer and scoreboard (Team Sara vs Team Omar)
student: Scissors (optional) to cut 12 paper morpheme cards: un-, re-, -er, -est, -ful, -less, -ness, -ment, -ion, help, care, kind

stages.name: Warm-up: Word Explosion
stages.purpose: Show that one small word can grow into a big family, and get teens competing from minute one.
teacherSays: One word on the screen: HELP. In 60 seconds, how many words can you make from it? Go!
Let's see... helpful, helpless, helper, helping, helped, unhelpful! Six words from one!
How did you do it? You added pieces. Today you become Word Builders: you'll learn the pieces and how to use them.
teacherSaysAr: كم كلمة تستطيع أن تصنع من help في 60 ثانية؟
صنعتم كلمات جديدة بإضافة قطع. اليوم ستصبحون بُناة كلمات!
studentsDo: Type all the words they can build from help in the chat in 60 seconds.
Count: the student with the most correct words gets the title 'Master Builder'.
tips: Accept inflections (helps, helped, helping) but point out they are 'grammar pieces' while helpful/helper are 'new-word pieces'.
If the group is slow, give the first two pieces as hints: -ful, -er.

stages.name: Discovery: Morpheme Surgery
stages.method: Guided discovery (segmenting words into morphemes and inferring meanings)
stages.purpose: Students learn the term morpheme, split real words into pieces and work out what each prefix and suffix means.
teacherSays: Put on your surgeon's gloves! We're going to cut words into their smallest meaningful pieces. Linguists call them morphemes.
Example: unhelpful. un + help + ful. Three morphemes. What does un mean? Not. What does ful mean? Full of. So unhelpful = not full of help!
Careful: you can't cut 'under' into un + der. Der means nothing. A morpheme must have a meaning.
Now you operate. Cut each word and tell me the meaning of each piece.
teacherSaysAr: المورفيم أصغر قطعة في الكلمة لها معنى.
لا نقطع إلا إذا كان لكل قطعة معنى: under ليست un + der.
studentsDo: Draw slashes between morphemes on paper (un/help/ful).
Write the meaning of each prefix and suffix in a table: un- = not, re- = again, -ful = full of, -less = without, -ness = state of, -er = person who / more.
Check answers with a partner and explain one in Arabic.

exercise.instructions: Cut the word into morphemes. How many pieces? What does each piece mean?
exercise.instructionsAr: قسّم الكلمة إلى مورفيمات. كم قطعة؟ وما معنى كل قطعة؟

items.answer: un + happi + ness (3): not + happy + state of
teach + er + s (3): teach + person who + plural
suggest + ion (2): suggest + noun (the thing suggested)
big + est (2, with double g): big + the most
play + er + s (3): play + person who + plural

tips: Accept 'happi' as happy with y → i: spelling changes don't change the morpheme.
Ask 'Is it a new word or a grammar form?' to separate -er (teacher) from -s (plural).

stages.name: Linguistics Corner + Arabic Bridge: Lego vs Weaving
stages.nameAr: ركن اللغويات وجسر العربية: الليغو مقابل النسيج
stages.method: Contrastive analysis using students' Arabic expertise (students teach the teacher)
stages.purpose: Compare English affixation with Arabic root-and-pattern morphology and show that students already have strong morphological skills from Arabic.
teacherSays: English builds words like Lego: you see the base, and you glue bricks to the front and back. happy, unhappy, unhappiness.
Arabic is a weaving language. You are the experts here! What do these words share: كاتب، مكتوب، مكتب، مكتبة، كتاب، كَتَبَ?
Yes, ك ت ب, the idea of writing. The root letters stay in order, and the pattern weaves vowels and letters between and around them.
And patterns have meanings, like suffixes! فاعِل: the person who does it. كاتب = writer, لاعب = player. Look: Arabic فاعِل is like English -er!
مَفْعَل and مَفْعَلة: a place. ملعب, مدرسة, مكتبة. English has no regular place pattern like this (only a few endings, like -ery in bakery): it says playground, school, library.
So Arabic speakers are already great at finding roots. Use that skill in English: find the base inside the long word!
teacherSaysAr: أنتم الخبراء هنا! ما المشترك بين كاتب ومكتوب ومكتب ومكتبة وكتاب؟ الجذر ك ت ب.
وزن فاعِل يشبه اللاحقة -er، ووزن مَفْعَل يدل على المكان.
مهارتكم في استخراج الجذر في العربية تساعدكم على إيجاد الأصل في الكلمات الإنجليزية الطويلة.
studentsDo: Find the root of each Arabic word and give the English equivalent.
Say which English piece (if any) does the same job as the Arabic pattern.
Build the ل-ع-ب family together on the whiteboard (لعب، لاعب، ملعب، لعبة، ألعاب).

exercise.instructions: Find the Arabic root. Then give the English word and say how English builds it.
exercise.instructionsAr: استخرج الجذر العربي، ثم اذكر الكلمة الإنجليزية وكيف تبنيها الإنجليزية.

items.answer: ل ع ب → playground / playing field (compounds built on play)
ك ت ب → written (write + -en, with a vowel change)
ك ت ب → library (a different word, not built from write)
ن ص ح → advice (a different word; the verb is advise)
ح ك م → judge (Lesson 10; the same form is a verb and a noun in English: to judge / a judge)

tips: Let students lead the Arabic part; teens love being the experts.
Be honest: Arabic also has prefixes and suffixes (ال، ـون، ـات), and English has a few inside changes (sing / sang, man / men). The difference is in what each language does most.
Strong students may notice that مُدَرِّس is not on فاعِل: it is مُفَعِّل, from the verb دَرَّسَ (to teach). Accept and praise.

stages.name: Affix Lab: Meaning and Word Class
stages.nameAr: مختبر السوابق واللواحق: المعنى ونوع الكلمة
stages.method: Concept table + gap-fill with word families
stages.purpose: Understand that prefixes change meaning while most suffixes also change the word class (verb → noun, noun → adjective), then use the right form in a sentence.
teacherSays: Prefixes change the meaning: happy → unhappy, write → rewrite. The word class stays the same.
Suffixes often change the job of the word. -ful and -less make adjectives: helpful, careless. -ness, -ion and -ment make nouns: kindness, suggestion, improvement. -er makes a person: teacher.
So when you choose a form, ask: what job does the sentence need here? A noun? An adjective? A verb?
Let's try with Lesson 12 words: improve, suggest, patience.
teacherSaysAr: السوابق تغيّر المعنى، أما كثير من اللواحق فتغيّر نوع الكلمة: فعل ← اسم، اسم ← صفة.
اسأل نفسك: ما الوظيفة المطلوبة هنا؟ اسم أم صفة أم فعل؟
studentsDo: Complete a table: verb / noun / adjective for help, care, use, suggest, improve.
Fill each gap with the right form of the word in brackets.
Say why: 'We need an adjective before the noun.'

exercise.instructions: Use the word in brackets in the correct form. Add a prefix or suffix.
exercise.instructionsAr: استخدم الكلمة بين القوسين بالشكل الصحيح، وأضف سابقة أو لاحقة.

items.prompt: Thanks for the tip. It's really (use).
Ziad made a (care) mistake on his test.
The waiter made a great (suggest): try the dessert!
I can see a big (improve) in your writing.
Your essay has mistakes. Please (write) it.
Noor is never angry. Her (kind) is famous.
Hamad hates waiting. He is very (patient).
The judge said the song was (popular) with young people. Nobody liked it.
Without a map we felt totally (help).

tips: impatient uses im- because patient starts with p (im- before p, b, m: impossible, imbalance). Mention briefly; don't overload.
Highlight that -ful has one l (useful), even though full has two: a classic spelling trap.

stages.name: Word-Building Race
stages.method: Team race with morpheme cards (gamified production)
stages.purpose: Build words fast from meanings, combining bases and affixes, under friendly time pressure.
teacherSays: Race time! Team Sara versus Team Omar. I give a meaning; you build the word from the cards and type it.
Example: 'a person who judges a talent show'... judge! Careful, some words don't need a suffix!
First correct spelling wins 1 point. Wrong spelling? The other team can steal.
teacherSaysAr: أعطيكم المعنى وأنتم تبنون الكلمة من البطاقات وتكتبونها.
studentsDo: Combine cards on the whiteboard or on paper and hold them up to the camera.
Type the full word in the chat.
Use 3 of the new words in one silly sentence for a bonus point.

exercise.instructions: Read the meaning. Build the word with a base + prefix/suffix.
exercise.instructionsAr: اقرأ المعنى وابنِ الكلمة من الأصل مع سابقة أو لاحقة.

items.prompt: not happy, and the noun of it

tips: talented uses -ed, not -ful: a nice surprise that shows English is not 100% regular.
recommendation: -ion often comes as -ation (recommend → recommendation, inform → information), and the stress moves (recomMEND → recommenDAtion). Say it with the class; suffixes can move stress.

stages.name: Spelling Surgeon: -er and -est
stages.method: Rule discovery from examples + sorting + error check
stages.purpose: Apply the three spelling rules when adding -er/-est (doubling, y → i, drop e) and know the irregular 'good, better, best'.
teacherSays: When we glue -er and -est, sometimes the word changes shape. Look: big → biggest, happy → happiest, nice → nicest. What happened?
Rule 1: short word, one short vowel + one consonant at the end → double it: big, biggest; hot, hottest.
Rule 2: consonant + y → change y to i: happy, happiest; funny, funniest.
Rule 3: silent e at the end → just add -r or -st: nice, nicest; large, largest.

And the rebels: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst. They come from completely different old words. Linguists call this suppletion. Arabic has something similar: for جيّد we often say أفضل, from a different root (ف ض ل)!
teacherSaysAr: قاعدة 1: حرف علة قصير + ساكن واحد ← نضاعف الساكن.
قاعدة 2: ساكن + y ← نحوّل y إلى i.
قاعدة 3: e صامتة في الآخر ← نضيف -r أو -st فقط.
good و bad شاذتان لأن أشكالهما جاءت من كلمات قديمة مختلفة.
studentsDo: Write the -er and -est forms and name the rule (1, 2, 3 or rebel).
Spot the misspelled superlatives on the 'talent show results' slide.

exercise.instructions: Write the superlative (the ___est). Which rule did you use?
exercise.instructionsAr: اكتب صيغة التفضيل العليا. أي قاعدة استخدمت؟

items.answer: the cheapest (no change: two vowels before p)
the most popular (long adjective: most, not -est)

tips: cheap does not double the p because it has two vowel letters (ea) before it: a good test of rule 1.
Remind students that long adjectives (popular, talented, impressive) use most: -est is for short words (one syllable, or two syllables ending in -y like happy and funny).

stages.name: Production: Talent Show Judges
stages.method: Creative role-play (task with a word-building checklist)
stages.purpose: Use built words naturally in speech: judges give comments and advice using affixed words and superlatives.
teacherSays: You are the judges of the Lumio Talent Show! Each of you writes a 4-sentence comment for an act: Lumi's dance, Ziad's magic trick or Sara's song.
Your comment must use: one un- word, one -ful or -less word, one -ness or -ment word, and one superlative. And some advice with should!
Example: 'Lumi, that was the funniest dance tonight! You were fearless and unstoppable. I can see a big improvement since last week. You should work on your timing.'
teacherSaysAr: أنتم حكّام برنامج المواهب! اكتبوا تعليقاً من 4 جمل فيه: كلمة بـ un-، وكلمة بـ -ful أو -less، وكلمة بـ -ness أو -ment، وصيغة تفضيل، ونصيحة بـ should.
studentsDo: Write a 4-sentence judge's comment with the checklist.
Read it aloud dramatically; the others tick the checklist and award applause points.
Vote for the most creative comment.
tips: Write the checklist on the slide and let students tick their own words before speaking.
Encourage kind feedback: the judges should be helpful, not hurtful (a nice -ful pair!).

stages.name: Exit Ticket and Did You Know?
stages.purpose: Check segmenting, affix meaning, spelling and the English/Arabic contrast individually.
teacherSays: Exit ticket: five items, privately to me in the chat.

Did you know? One of the longest words in English dictionaries, 'antidisestablishmentarianism', is just Lego: anti + dis + establish + ment + arian + ism. And Arabic can pack a whole sentence into one word: وسيكتبونها (and they will write it) = و + سـ + يـ + كتب + ون + ها, built on our old friend ك ت ب!
Mission: find a long English word this week and cut it into morphemes.
teacherSaysAr: هل تعلم؟ من أطول الكلمات الإنجليزية antidisestablishmentarianism، وهي مجرد قطع ليغو! والعربية تستطيع أن تجمع جملة كاملة في كلمة واحدة: «وسيكتبونها» = و + سـ + يـ + كتب + ون + ها، من صديقنا القديم ك ت ب!
مهمتك: ابحث عن كلمة إنجليزية طويلة هذا الأسبوع وقسّمها إلى مورفيمات.
studentsDo: Answer 5 items privately.
Share one word they built today that they really like.
tips: Note who confuses word classes (use vs useful); revisit with quick 'word family' warm-ups in Lessons 13-16.

items.prompt: How many morphemes are in 'careless'? Name them.
Complete: Thank you! Your advice is very ___ (use).
Which Arabic pattern means 'the person who does it', like English -er?

homework.en: Word Family Poster: choose 2 bases (for example help and kind, or care and use) and build a family tree with at least 5 words for each, labelled noun / verb / adjective. Then build one Arabic root family (for example ل ع ب or د ر س) with 5 words and write the English meaning of each. Finish with 5 sentences that use one word from each family.
homework.ar: ملصق عائلة الكلمات: اختر أصلين (مثل help و kind أو care و use) وابنِ لكل منهما شجرة عائلة من 5 كلمات على الأقل، واكتب نوع كل كلمة (اسم / فعل / صفة). ثم ابنِ عائلة جذر عربي (مثل ل ع ب أو د ر س) من 5 كلمات واكتب معناها بالإنجليزية. واختم بـ 5 جمل.
tasks: Two English word-family trees (5+ words each) with word classes.
One Arabic root family (5 words) with English meanings.
Five sentences using the new words.
Bonus: find one English word with three or more morphemes in a book, a game or an app.

support: Give a reference card with the meaning of each affix and an example.
In the race, show the base word and ask only for the affix.
For spelling, focus on rule 2 (y → i) and the rebel good/best first.
challenge: Find words with two prefixes or two suffixes (re + un + ...; care + less + ness = carelessness).
Investigate -er with two jobs: list 5 comparatives and 5 'person' words and explain how you can tell them apart.
Compare: Arabic مكتبة can mean a library or a bookshop, but English uses two words. Why might a language use one word for both?

successCriteria: Segments at least 8 of 10 words into morphemes correctly.
Chooses the right word form in at least 8 of 10 gap-fills.
Spells at least 7 of 9 superlatives correctly and names the rule.
Explains the difference between English affixation and Arabic root-and-pattern morphology in 1-2 sentences.
Uses at least four built words correctly in the judge's comment.
watchFor: Wrong word class (very use, a care driver, I want to improvement)
the most big / more good / the goodest
Separate 'not' instead of a prefix (very not patient)
Cutting words into pieces with no meaning (un + der)

teacherNotes: The class uses Lesson 9-12 vocabulary (talented, popular, judge, suggest, recommend, improve, advice, patience, mistake, cheap) as raw material for word building.
Celebrate Arabic morphology: Arabic-speaking students are often excellent at finding roots, which transfers well to English word families.
Keep the 'concatenative / non-concatenative' terms for the teacher and strong students; for most, 'Lego vs weaving' is enough.
The word وسيكتبونها shows that Arabic also glues pieces (و، سـ، يـ، ـون، ـها) around a pattern-built stem: a good reminder that both languages mix the two methods.
Bonus Class 4 moves from words to how we use them with people: politeness and register.
